title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: St. Joseph leaders debate a moratorium while residents from Saline to Palmyra push back on power and water costs.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into St. Joseph County's debate over a possible two-year freeze on new data center projects.
That sounds like it could ripple across southwest Michigan.
Exactly. County leaders are looking at a moratorium to block new proposals while they study impacts on roads, water, and electricity.
Why now? What's driving this push for a pause?
Residents nearby are worried about higher utility bills and losing farmland to these big facilities.
That makes sense with everything else we're hearing this week.
A decision here could really set the tone for other townships in the region.
Let's unpack the bigger picture. How long has this tension been building?
It's been accelerating fast. Just yesterday we saw pushback in places like Palmyra Township in Lenawee County, where neighbors raised noise and power cost fears during a zoning session.
And in Vevay Township, landowners are actually pushing for annexation into Mason to clear the way for a project.
Right, that would shift tax revenue and control from the township to the city.
So the stakes for local control are huge.
They are. And former congressman Mike Rogers came out yesterday saying Michigan should halt new data centers to avoid spiking power costs.
He's pointing to the strain on utilities from all these AI projects.
Exactly. One township even blocked new power lines to stop a University of Michigan-linked hyperscale project.
That one tied to Los Alamos too, right? Residents don't want massive infrastructure without local say.
Correct. It directly affects nearby homes and farms by cutting off the grid connection.
How does all this affect electric bills for people 30 or 60 miles away?
The added power demand from these facilities can raise rates across the grid. That's why Rogers and others are calling for limits.
What about water use? These places need a lot, don't they?
They do. Cooling systems pull significant amounts, which worries communities already concerned about resources.
And farmland — once it's built, it's gone for good.
That's the fear in St. Joseph and places like Saline, where dozens packed a coffee hour today to question leaders.
What did they focus on there?
Higher electric bills, water use, and lost tax revenue if projects get big tax breaks.
So it's not just environmental — it's pocketbook issues too.
Precisely. And in Saline Township, the developer behind one big campus just bought the neighboring golf course.
That signals they might want to expand the footprint even more.
Residents are watching that closely, wondering what it means for pending reviews.
Meanwhile, Hyperscale Data sold $43 million in Bitcoin today to fund their Michigan buildout.
They offloaded 685 BTC and cut debt by $30 million, all earmarked for the project.
Crypto volatility directly funding local infrastructure — that's a new wrinkle.
It shows how these projects tie into broader markets.
And OpenAI-Oracle's developer also snapped up a golf course beside their planned campus.
Same pattern: buying adjacent land despite local pushback over noise, traffic, and power draw.
Washtenaw County projects are moving forward but under tighter local oversight now.
Boards there are setting rules on size and location instead of waiting for state action.
What happens next in St. Joseph if they approve this freeze?
It would pause new proposals for two years while they study the impacts.
That gives time to look at roads, water, and electricity strain.
And it could influence how other southwest Michigan townships handle similar proposals.
Do we know how many places have already paused or tightened rules?
It's spreading quickly — we've seen moves in Washtenaw, Lenawee, and now this potential in St. Joseph.
Any sense of what a typical data center pulls in power?
These hyperscale ones can demand enormous amounts, enough to strain local grids and push up costs for everyone.
So the decision in St. Joseph really matters beyond the county line.
It does. Residents 30 miles away could feel it through their bills.
And the developers are clearly positioning for growth.
That's why today's coffee hour in Saline and the zoning talks elsewhere feel connected.
The issue is becoming a flashpoint fast.
Now let's hit some of the other stories making waves this week.
Starting with Saline — residents there are already voicing fears over power and tax costs at that packed session today.
Dozens showed up to question leaders directly.
And yesterday in Palmyra, neighbors focused on electric bills and constant noise.
Officials heard those concerns during the public zoning session.
Anyone within 50 miles could face higher utility costs if projects advance without limits.
Meanwhile, Vevay Township landowners are pushing annexation to move forward with their plans.
That would shift tax revenue and local control to the city of Mason.
Residents in Lansing or Jackson could see new power and water demand from that one.
In Washtenaw, the weekly roundup shows oversight expanding as proposals advance.
Local boards tightening rules rather than waiting on the state.
And that Rogers comment yesterday — he told Detroit voters a temporary halt makes sense.
Citing the strain on Michigan utilities from AI demand.
The township blocking power lines to stop the U-M project is another big one from yesterday.
Residents there don't want to lose say over infrastructure serving a facility linked to national labs.
No major meetings on the calendar for tonight or tomorrow that we've confirmed.
Listeners should check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for any last-minute additions.
Always good to stay on top of those local agendas.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening.

episode_title: St. Joseph County Weighs Two-Year Data Center Freeze as Statewide Concerns Mount
